step1_summary: Chief complaint: Progressive anxiety over the past ≈2 months, worst in the mornings before work.

Symptoms: • Onset ≈2 months, coinciding with a new, stressful job. • Daily dread of leaving the house/going to work. • Marked insomnia (goes to bed 22-23 h, sleeps ≈3–4 h, shallow). • Morning palpitations (irregular, last minutes–10 min, associated with fear of heart attack). • Low daytime energy, anhedonia, avoidance of friends/hobbies, reduced exercise. • No true panic attacks yet; no suicidal ideation.
Aggravating factors: Thoughts of work, fear of being late.  Alleviating factors: none clearly stated.
Family history: Mother with a history of depression.
Social history: Lives with parents. Alcohol: binges on Fri/Sat, occasional weekday wine; amount likely above recommended limits. Occasional smoker. No recreational drugs.
Labs/Imaging: None yet; GP plans basic bloods (unspecified).

V: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) or atrial fibrillation: Could explain episodic palpitations and perceived irregular fast heart beat.
I: Subacute (viral) myocarditis: Can present with palpitations and fatigue, although no infective prodrome reported.
N: Pheochromocytoma: Catecholamine surges cause episodic palpitations, anxiety, insomnia.
D: Iron-deficiency anaemia: Causes fatigue, palpitations, low energy.
I2: Caffeine / alcohol-induced anxiety-palpitations: Regular alcohol binges and possible caffeine use could precipitate symptoms.
C: Mitral valve prolapse: Congenital/structural cause of palpitations often associated with anxiety.
A: Graves’ disease (autoimmune hyperthyroidism): Produces anxiety, insomnia, palpitations, weight change.
T: Work-related psychological stress (adjustment reaction): Emotional ‘trauma’ from hostile workplace triggering anxiety.
E: Generalised anxiety disorder / mixed anxiety-depressive disorder: Endocrine-metabolic ‘E’ category broadened here to psychiatric aetiology; fits chronic worry, somatic tension, sleep disturbance.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Adjustment disorder with anxiety (early Generalised Anxiety Disorder)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Clear temporal relationship to starting a new stressful job; pervasive worry, restlessness, sleep disturbance, physical tension and functional impairment without prior history.
supporting_evidence: Onset within 2 months of new job.
Excessive daily worry about work and performance.
Functional impact: dread leaving house, reduced enjoyment of hobbies, social withdrawal.
opposing_evidence: Duration <6 months (strict GAD DSM-5 criterion), though adjustment disorder criteria are met.
Still able to attend work daily (function not completely lost).

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Low mood, anhedonia, fatigue and insomnia on most days for several weeks suggest evolving depressive episode, possibly comorbid with anxiety.
supporting_evidence: Reports feeling ‘down’ most of the time, even on weekends.
Marked anhedonia (no enjoyment in running, tennis, friends).
opposing_evidence: Primary complaint is anxiety; depressive features may be secondary.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Thyrotoxicosis can mimic anxiety with palpitations and insomnia; easily screened on planned blood tests.
supporting_evidence: Palpitations and anxiety out of proportion to situation.
Plan for blood work indicates clinician concern.
opposing_evidence: No weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, diarrhoea, or neck swelling reported.
Symptoms started with identifiable psychosocial stressor.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Episodic irregular rapid heartbeat lasting minutes could be arrhythmia rather than anxiety.
supporting_evidence: Subjective description of ‘irregular’ rapid heartbeat lasting up to 10 min.
Fear of heart attack on waking.
opposing_evidence: Attacks closely linked to anticipatory anxiety about work.
No syncope, chest pressure, known heart disease.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Could cause fatigue and palpitations; simple to rule out with blood tests.
opposing_evidence: No menstrual or dietary history suggesting deficiency.
Onset coincides with identifiable psychosocial trigger.
